synthesisReport.summary: The Give-to-Get Hypothesis aims to provide founders and indie developers with a platform where access to feedback is granted only after they have given detailed feedback on other participants' projects. The hypothesis is supported by the need for honest feedback in the market, as evident from the high demand for customer feedback software and the growing adoption of 360-degree feedback in various industries. However, the comments also reveal skepticism about the effectiveness of the reciprocity mechanic and concerns about the quality of feedback. The platform distribution shows that Reddit is the dominant platform, with a positive sentiment score of 0.1. The recent activity level is high, with a score of 0.8, and the trend direction is increasing.
recommendations: Conduct user interviews to test key assumptions about the effectiveness of the reciprocity mechanic and the quality of feedback.
Develop a landing page or fake-door to measure interest and willingness to participate in the give-to-get feedback platform.
Create a community experiment on Reddit to observe user behavior and engagement in the platform.
Pivot the platform to focus on a different segment, such as product managers or entrepreneurs, based on the insights gained from the user interviews and community experiment.

projectHypothesis: If we offer founders and indie developers a platform where access to feedback on their projects is granted only after they have given detailed feedback on other participants' projects (give-to-get), then within the first 30 days: at least 200 users will register; 60% of them will complete at least one "gave feedback — received feedback" cycle; the average number of comments per project will be at least 5; 75% of users will rate the usefulness of the feedback received as 4 or 5 on a 5-point scale — because founders acutely need honest feedback but existing channels (friends, forums) do not provide it in sufficient volume and quality; the reciprocity mechanic creates a fair exchange and motivates participation; and research shows that advising others benefits the advisor ("learning-by-advising").
